title: Regulation of Amino Acid Transporters and Sensors in Response to a High protein Diet: A Randomized Controlled Trial in Elderly Men
journal: The Journal of Nutrition, Health & Aging

sections.abstract:
The mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) is fundamental for many cellular processes, yet it is often dysregulated with aging. Increased amino acid (AA) availability is correlated with the expression of AA transporters (AAT) and mTORC1 activity. Although many AA sensors and mediators have been proposed to relay the AA signal to mTORC1, it has not yet been determined if chronic dietary intervention affects the expression of AAT, sensors and mediators and their relationships with mTORC1 activity.

This study investigated whether the consumption of a diet containing either the current recommended daily allowance (RDA) of protein intake (0.8 g/kg/d) or twice the RDA (2RDA) for ten weeks affected the expression of targets associated with AA transport, sensing and mTORC1 regulation in 26 older men (70-81 years).

Muscle biopsies were collected before and after the intervention under fasting conditions. Diets were controlled by providing fully prepared meals and snacks. Western blot and quantitative polymerase chain reaction were used to measure protein and gene expression respectively.

Consumption of 2RDA reduced the protein expression of L-type amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1). However, plasma leucine concentration and basal mTORC1 activity were unaltered. The downregulation of LAT1 did not affect the expression of AA sensors and mediators, including leucyl tRNA synthetase (LRS), cytosolic arginine sensor for mTORC1 (CASTOR1), Sestrin2 and Rag proteins. Instead, total ribosomal protein S6 (RPS6) was upregulated with 2RDA.

Ten weeks of 2RDA diet did not affect the fasting mTORC1 signaling, but increased total RPS6 might suggest improved muscular translational capacity to maintain muscular mass.

Key words: Aging, amino acid, dietary protein, mTORC1, skeletal muscle
sections.introduction:
Skeletal muscle is vital for movement and metabolism ( 1 , 2 ). Muscle mass and function gradually decline from middleage ( 3 ), and this loss is associated with impaired whole-body insulin sensitivity ( 4 ) and physical mobility ( 5 ). The importance of adequate dietary protein to preserve muscle mass ( 6 , 7 ) and lower type 2 diabetes risk ( 8 ) has been demonstrated. Yet, this may be difficult in the elderly who frequently experience reduced chewing efficiency ( 9 ), poor appetite ( 10 ), and delayed amino acid (AA) absorption ( 11 ), thus increasing the likelihood of insufficient dietary protein intake ( 12 , 13 ). Currently 0.8 g/kg/d of protein is the recommended daily allowance (RDA) established by the World Health Organization (WHO) ( 14 ) and the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) ( 15 ). However, recommendations vary by jurisdiction. For example, in Australia and New Zealand, older men (age >70 years) are recommended to consume a diet containing 1.07 g protein/kg/d ( 16 ). We and others have demonstrated the importance of protein intake for both skeletal muscle mass and function with levels twice the RDA (1.6 g/kg/d) in older individuals ( 7 , 17 ). However, these data do not describe the intramuscular molecular mechanisms that are regulated in response to altered dietary protein intake.

The mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signaling is fundamental for muscle protein synthesis (MPS), cell growth, metabolism, autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis ( 18 , 19 , 20 ). In rats, mice and older adults, mTORC1 becomes hyperactive with age ( 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ). Chronic mTORC1 activation is associated with age-related disorders, including insulin resistance, metabolic diseases, inflammation and cancer ( 20 , 25 , 26 ). There is little data available on whether habitual diet can also alter mTORC1 activity in older men.

Essential AAs (EAA) are potent stimulators of the mTORC1 pathway ( 19 , 27 ), but the mechanistic regulation of AA-dependent mTORC1 activation is complex. Amino acid transporters (AAT) play critical roles in both nutrient sensing and intracellular signaling ( 28 ). The expression of skeletal muscle AATs is known to respond to various stimuli ( 29 ). Of the AATs, expression of L-type amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1), sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter (SNAT2), cationic amino acid transporter (CAT1) and proton assisted amino acid transporter (PAT1) have all been demonstrated to increase in response to combined dietary protein ingestion and resistance exercise ( 30 , 31 ). Modifying diet alone did not alter LAT1/SLC7A5 and SNAT2/SLC38A2 mRNA in young adults ingesting up to three times the RDA for ten days ( 32 ). It is possible that longer dietary interventions are required to impact AAT expression.

Further downstream of AATs are the Ras-related GTP binding proteins A-D (Rag A-D) which are necessary for the translocation of mTORC1 to the lysosome for activation in response to protein feeding ( 33 , 34 ). The current theory is that Rag proteins are regulated through multiple pathways, either via leucyl-tRNA synthetase (LRS) ( 35 , 36 ), the solute carrier 38A9 (SLC38A9) ( 37 , 38 , 39 ), or the GTPase activator protein activity towards Rags (GATOR2) ( 40 , 41 ). Additionally, Sestrin2, a putative leucine sensor, and cytosolic arginine sensor for mTORC1 (CASTOR1) are proposed to regulate GATOR2 (42- 45). There is scarce data on the regulation of these mechanisms and pathways in human skeletal muscle, including the analysis of dietary responsiveness.

Our laboratory has previously shown that consuming the current RDA for protein reduced appendicular lean mass and grip strength while consuming 2RDA maintained appendicular lean mass and increased whole-body lean mass and knee extensor power in healthy older men ( 7 ). An increase in dietary protein supplementation has been demonstrated to increase the expression of AATs and mTORC1 activity in young adults ( 46 , 47 ). Similarly, leucine-enriched EAA supplementation after resistance exercise induced AATs and prolonged the anabolic response in older adults ( 30 ), hence we hypothesized that the consumption of a well-controlled diet containing 2RDA of protein for ten weeks in older men (70-81 years) would increase the expression levels of AATs and mTORC1 activity following an overnight fast when compared to participants consuming the RDA for protein. Further, we hypothesized a similar change in the expression of AA sensors and mediators would be observed.
sections.methods:
Participants, a subset of a larger study ( 7 ), were non-smokers who had a BMI ranging from 18 to 35 kg/m2 and did not take any dietary supplements for at least one month preceding the study. All participants were able to perform daily activities independently without mobility aids. Those with restricted eating habits, including vegetarians and those with food allergies, were excluded. Three of the original 29 participants ( 7 ) were excluded from this study as there was insufficient remaining tissue from muscle biopsies. Participants habitually consumed on average more protein (~1.1-1.2 g/kg/d) than the elderly New Zealand males (> 70 y) (~1.0 g/kg/d) ( 16 ). Fourteen men randomly assigned to the RDA group were provided with a controlled diet that contained 0.8 g protein/ kg/d for ten weeks. Twelve men assigned to the 2RDA group received 1.6 g protein/kg/d. All participants consumed 28-31% of energy from fat. The difference in the balance of energy intake was made up of carbohydrate.

Participant characteristics are shown in Table 1 . A detailed description of the diet has been published previously ( 7 ). Briefly, the energy content of the diet was individually calculated to match participants’ estimated energy needs based on the Harris-Benedict equation and adjusted for physical activity, which was assessed by wrist-worn accelerometers (Fitbit Charge HR). Throughout the study, protein and energy were distributed between breakfast, lunch and dinner as 30%, 30% and 40% respectively. All food consumed by the participants during the ten week intervention was provided by investigators, except black coffee and tea. During the intervention, participants maintained their normal lifestyle and all meals were provided in a prepared form requiring only reheating or minimal preparation by participants. Recommendations for intake of fruit and vegetables were met and dietary records were completed at 5, 6, 9 and 10 weeks and food selection were adjusted to participants’ preferences. Compliance exceeded 97% for protein and energy intake in both groups ( 7 ).

Subject characteristics

Values are means ± standard deviation. The RDA is 0.8 g protein/kg/d; 2RDA is 1.6 g protein/kg/d BMI, Body mass index, RDA, Recommended daily allowance.

All participants were informed of the requirements and potential risks of the studies prior to providing written informed consent. The experimental procedures adhered to the standards set by the latest version of the Declaration of Helsinki and were approved by the Southern Health and Disability Ethics Committee (New Zealand; 15/STH/236). The study was registered with the Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trial Registry as ACTRN12616000310460.

At least three days prior to the beginning of the ten weeks dietary intervention, participants were asked to refrain from intense physical activity, and on the evening before the study, participants were instructed to consume their regular diet before 10 pm and consume nothing except water for the rest of the evening. Participants arrived fasted at the University of Auckland Nutrition and Mobility Clinic at approximately 7 am. A cannula was inserted into an arm vein and a baseline blood sample was collected. A muscle biopsy was obtained from the vastus lateralis of a random leg (counterbalanced for dominance) under local anaesthesia (1% Xylocaine) using a Bergstrom needle modified for manual suction. Biopsies were quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80°C until further analyses. Following the ten week dietary intervention period, participants returned to the laboratory after an overnight fast for the collection of a second muscle biopsy from the other leg and baseline blood sample.

For plasma analysis, ultra-high pressure liquid chromatography (UHPLC) was used to determine plasma AA concentration as previously described ( 48 ). Briefly, 20 μL of plasma was deproteinized via tungstate precipitation by mixing with 160 μL of 0.04 M H2SO4 (containing 15 μM of norvaline as the internal standard) and 20 μL of 10% Na2WO4 (sodium tungstate). Supernatant was collected after centrifugation at 14,000 g for 10 min at 4°C. Plasma AA concentration was then measured by a fluorescent derivitization, utilizing the reaction of aminonitrogen with 6-aminoquinolyl-N-hydroxysuccinimidyl carbonate and subsequent separation by UHPLC. Data were captured by computer with Chromeleon 7.1 software (Thermo Scientific). Standard curves for each AA were used to calculate plasma AA concentrations.

For protein analysis, approximately 20 mg of muscle tissue were homogenized with 1x RIPA lysis buffer (Millipore, Temecula, CA, USA, no. 20-188) with added Halt TM protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA, no. 78442). Supernatants were collected after centrifugation at 15,000 g for 10 min at 4°C and total protein concentration was determined using the Pierce TM BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Scientific, no.23225). Muscle homogenate was diluted to a concentration of 2 μg/ μl with water and Laemmli buffer then heated at 95°C for 5 min. 20 μg of protein was loaded onto SDS-PAGE gels for protein separation by electrophoresis and transferred to PVDF membranes (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Inc., CA, USA, no.170-4157) using the semidry Trans-Blot Turbo TM device (Bio-Rad). Membranes were blocked for 1 h at room temperature in 5% bovine serum albumin in Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween 20 (TBST). Then they were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies at 1: 1,000 dilution. The following antibodies were used: LAT1 (#5347), RagB (#8150), RagD (#4470), p70S6K1 (#2708), PRAS40 (#2691), p-p70S6K1 Thr421/Ser424 (#9204), p-eIF4E Ser209 (#9741), p-PRAS40 Thr246 (#13175), total RPS6 (#2317) and p-RPS6 Ser235/236 (#2211) from (Cell Signalling Technology, Inc., Danvers, MA) and total eIF4E (sc- 9976) and SNAT2 (sc-67081) from (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA). The next day, after washing in TBST, membranes were incubated with appropriate anti-rabbit or anti-mouse secondary antibodies (Jackson Immuno Research Laboratories, PA) linked to horseradish peroxidase (1:10,000) for 1 h at room temperature. The membranes were washed again and antibody binding was visualized using ECL select western blotting detection reagent (ECL Select kit; GE Healthcare Ltd., Little Chalfont, UK) and chemiluminescent signals were captured using a ChemiDoc™ MP Imaging System (Bio-Rad, Hongkong, China). Bands were quantified using ImageJ software (NIH, Bethesda, MD). Western blot data were normalized to total protein, which was determined by staining with Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 Dye (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany). Phospho-proteins were normalized to their respective total protein. Due to insufficient sample volumes, protein data was available for 11 older men from the RDA group and 10 from the 2RDA group.

Following the manufacturer’s instructions from the AllPrep® DNA/RNA/miRNA Universal Kit (QIAGEN GmbH, Hilden, Germany), total RNA was extracted from ~20 mg of muscle tissues. RNA concentration was measured using the NanoPhotometer® N60 (IMPLEN, Inc., Westlake Village, CA, USA). To calculate RNA per mg of tissue (ng/mg), total eluted RNA (ng) was divided by the mass of the tissue it was extracted from (mg).

1,500 ng of input RNA was used for cDNA synthesis using High-Capacity RNA-to-cDNATM kit (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA). Messenger RNA (mRNA) was measured by RT-PCR on a LightCycler 480 II (Roche Applied Science, Penzberg, Germany) using SYBR Green I Master Mix (Roche Applied Science). Target mRNAs were LAT1/ SLC7A5 , SNAT2/ SLC38A2 , CAT1/ SLC7A1 , PAT1/ SLC36A1 , SLC38A9 , RRAGA , RRAGB , RRAGC , RRAGD , LRS , SESN1 , SESN2 , SESN3 , CASTOR1 , MIOS , WDR24 and LAPTM4b . Primers were designed using BLAST software ( 49 ) with sequences in Table 2 . Relative fold changes were determined using the 2 -ΔΔCT method ( 50 ). The geometric mean of five reference genes was used for normalization ( 51 ). The recently proposed human reference genes ( 52 ), chromosome 1 open reading frame 43 (C1orf43), charged multivesicular body protein 2A (CHMP2A), ER membrane protein complex subunit 7 (EMC7), heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) and hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase 1 (HPRT) were identified as the least variable and used as reference genes. Standard and melting curves were performed for every target to confirm primer efficiency and single-product amplification.

Primer sequences used for real-time quantitative RT-PCR

LAT, L-type amino acid transporter 1; SNAT, Sodium-couple amino acid transporter; CAT, Cationic amino acid transporter; PAT, Proton-coupled amino acid transporter; SLC38A9, Solute carrier family 38 member 9; RRAG, Ras related GTP-binding protein GTPase; LRS, Leucyl-tRNA synthetase; SESN, Sestrin; CASTOR1, Cytosolic arginine sensor for mTORC1; MIOS, Meiosis regulator for oocyte development; WDR24, WD repeat domain 24.

Differences in plasma AA concentration, protein and mRNA expressions were tested using two-way repeated measures ANOVA with time as a repeated fixed factor and group as a between-subject fixed factor. When interactions were observed, differences from baseline within each group and post-intervention between groups were analyzed using a Sidak post hoc test. When interaction was not present, and instead there was a main time or group effect, post hoc tests were performed on the marginal means. All analysis was conducted using SigmaPlot (Systat Software, Inc., San Jose, CA). For plasma AA concentration, raw values were used for analysis. For protein and mRNA data analysis, each subject was compared to themselves and pre-intervention samples were given an arbitrary expression of 1 and post-intervention values were represented as fold changes in respect to the prefeeding abundance ( 53 , 54 ). The study was powered based on the primary outcomes previously reported ( 7 ). Based on the variability we have previously reported in similar participants ( 55 , 56 ), the present study was powered to detect 35% difference in p70S6K1 phosphorylation and 30% difference in LAT1 mRNA expression with 80% power. Normality was determined using Shapiro-Wilk analysis. Where necessary, data were log-transformed to achieve normality. Significance was set at p<0.05 and data are shown as mean ± standard deviation (SD).
sections.results:
There were no significant changes over time for the concentration of total AA (p=0.37) or difference between groups (p=0.14). The concentration of non-essential amino acids (NEAA) tended to be different between groups postintervention (time × group p=0.06). Compared to the RDA group, the concentration of NEAA was lower in the 2RDA group (p=0.01). In particular, the concentrations of alanine and glycine were different (time × group p=0.01 and 0.04, respectively). Post-intervention, alanine was reduced in the 2RDA group (p=0.02), and glycine was reduced below that of the RDA group (p=0.02) ( Table 3 ). The concentration of serine was different between groups (p=0.03), but an effect of dietary intervention was not observed (p=0.13). The concentration of glutamine was different between groups (p<0.01) and increased after the dietary intervention (p=0.01), but interaction was not detected (time × group p=0.34).

Plasma amino acid profile

Values represent mean ± SD. Amino acid values measured in μmol/L. †Significant main effect, p<0.05. *Different from pre-intervention within the same group, p<0.05. #Different between diets at indicated time point, p<0.05.

There were no significant changes over time for the concentration of essential amino acids (EAA) (p=0.28) and they did not differ between groups (p=0.96). The concentration of branched chain amino acids (BCAA) tended to decrease in both groups (p=0.09) with no group difference (p=0.31). Individual analysis of BCAAs showed that the concentration of valine decreased with dietary intervention in both groups (p=0.04). While the concentration of isoleucine tended to decreased in both groups (p=0.08), there were no significant changes over time for the concentration of leucine (p=0.24) and it did not differ between groups (p=0.50).

LAT1/ SLC7A5 mRNA expression increased with dietary intervention (main effect of time p=0.03) with no difference between groups (p=0.38). CAT1/ SLC7A1 mRNA showed a tendency to be increased (p=0.06) and was not different between groups (p=0.19). There were no significant changes over time for SNAT2/ SLC38A2 , PAT1/ SLC36A1 and SLC38A9 mRNA expression (p=0.56, 0.33 and 0.79, respectively) and they did not differ between groups (p=0.34, 0.35 and 0.33, respectively; Figure 1A ). The protein expression of LAT1 was differentially expressed between the two groups (time × group p=0.04). LAT1 protein was reduced in the 2RDA group (p=0.02), but not in the RDA group (p=0.69). Compared to the RDA group, LAT1 protein was also lower in the 2RDA group (p=0.01). SNAT2 protein did not change post-intervention (p=0.15) or differ between groups (p=0.70; Figure 1B ).

Amino Acid Transporters and Sensors

The mRNA expression of LRS showed a tendency to be decreased with dietary intervention in both groups (p=0.055) with no group differences (p=0.32). SESN1/2/3 mRNA expression did not change over time (p=0.26, 0.12 and 0.36, respectively); or differ between groups (p=0.90, 0.55 and 0.32, respectively; Figure 1C ). The change in CASTOR1 mRNA showed a tendency to be different between groups (time × group p=0.06), its expression increased in the 2RDA group (p=0.01), but not the RDA group (p=1.00).

No significant change over time were found for the mRNA expression of RRAGA, RRAGB, RRAGC, RRAGD, MIOS and WDR24 (p=0.21, 0.51, 0.59, 0.58, 0.19 and 0.66, respectively) and they did not differ between groups (p=0.31, 0.93, 0.85, 0.68, 0.28 and 0.44, respectively; Figure 2A ). Rag B protein showed a tendency to be increased in both groups (p=0.06) but did not differ between groups (p=0.44). Rag D protein did not change post-intervention (p=0.98) and was not different between groups (p=0.23; Figure 2B ).

Rag Proteins and GATOR2

Phosphorylation of p70S6K1 Thr421/Ser424 , eIF4E Ser209 and PRAS40 Thr246 did not change following the intervention in either groups (p=0.40, 0.99 and 0.21, respectively) and did not differ between groups (p=0.23, 0.73 and 0.59, respectively). Similarly, total p70S6K1, eIF4E and PRAS40 did not change over time (p=0.46, 0.19 and 0.73) or differ between groups (p=0.47, 0.87 and 0.28, respectively) ( Figure 3A-B ). Phosphorylation of RPS6 Ser235/236 showed a tendency to be different between groups (time × group p=0.07); this was lower in the 2RDA group than the RDA group (p=0.01). The protein expression of RPS6 was different between groups (time × group p=0.03); it increased in the 2RDA group (p=0.02), but not the RDA group (p=0.49). Total RPS6 was also greater in the 2RDA group compared to the RDA group (p=0.01; Figure 4 ). Before the intervention, total RNA per mg of tissue was 335 ± 23 ng/ mg in the RDA group and 368 ± 24 ng/mg in the 2RDA group. The concentration did not change following the intervention in either groups (p=0.99) and did not differ between groups (p=0.20) (328 ± 20 ng/mg in the RDA group and 372 ± 27 ng/ mg in the 2RDA group).

sections.discussion:
Ten weeks of consuming a well-controlled diet containing twice the current RDA for protein intake decreased the fasting muscular protein expression of LAT1 and upregulated RPS6 protein. While the expression of other key skeletal muscle AATs, putative AA sensors and Rag family members necessary for mTORC1 regulation were not affected by the dietary intervention in older men (70-81 years). Previously published data from this study demonstrated that consuming a diet containing 2RDA for protein for ten weeks increased lean body mass and knee extensor power in older men, while a diet with RDA reduced appendicular lean mass and grip strength ( 7 ). mTORC1 signaling is fundamental for MPS and increased EAA availability postprandially correlates with acute changes in AATs, mTORC1 activity and regulation of skeletal muscle anabolism ( 57 , 58 , 59 ). In the present analysis, fasting plasma EAA concentration and mTORC1 downstream anabolic signaling was not affected by ten weeks of dietary intervention in older men.

The plasma concentration of valine reduced regardless of the interventions, while total BCAA concentration showed a tendency to be reduced. Plasma BCAA concentration has been reportedly altered in individuals with obesity, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, with obese individuals showing increased BCAA concentration ( 60 , 61 ). It has been suggested that elevated BCAA concentrations may exacerbate insulin resistance via mTORC1 hyperactivation ( 62 ). This is contradicted by the improvement in glucose homeostasis in type 2 diabetic individuals fed a BCAA-enriched meal ( 63 ). Further, instead of BCAAs, 3-hydroxyisobutyrate (3-HIB), a catabolic intermediate of valine, has been shown to be related to insulin sensitivity ( 64 ). In the present analysis, despite the reduction in valine concentration, mTORC1 anabolic signaling was not affected. Further, consistent with ( 65 ), long-term dietary protein intervention did not alter the insulin sensitivity of older men. As higher fasting BCAAs concentrations are related to metabolic dysregulation, the lack of increase in fasting BCAAs after a period of greatly increased protein intake suggested no causal link between protein consumption and metabolic dysregulation.

The expression levels of the following AATs: LAT1, SNAT2, CAT1, PAT1, and SLC38A9; were examined due to their close relationship with BCAAs and mTORC1 signaling ( 28 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 66 , 67 , 68 ). In response to the dietary intervention and compared to the RDA group, the plasma concentrations of alanine and glycine were reduced in the 2RDA group. However, the mRNA expression of SNAT2/SLC38A2, which transports alanine, glutamine and serine ( 69 ) and PAT1/ SLC36A1, which transports alanine, glycine and proline ( 70 ) did not change when analyzed in the skeletal muscle obtained by biopsy following an overnight fast. Instead, both groups showed increased mRNA expression of LAT1/SLC7A5. LAT1 operates as an obligatory 1:1 tertiary active exchanger, where it facilitates the uptake of BCAA (leucine, isoleucine and valine) with the efflux of cytoplasmic glutamine, which is accumulated via SNAT2 ( 28 ). The plasma concentration of glutamine was upregulated, while valine was downregulated in both groups. Whether the increased mRNA expression of LAT1/SLC7A5 facilitated an increased exchange between valine and glutamine is currently unknown since intracellular AA concentrations were not measured and samples were taken in fasting condition, where upregulation of AA transport would be minimal.

Interestingly, while the protein expression of SNAT2 was unaltered after the intervention, LAT1 was downregulated in the 2RDA group. Fractionating muscle homogenates and extracting the membrane fraction has been proposed to provide a clearer picture of the dynamic changes of AAT proteins ( 71 ). Such technique requires large amounts of starting material while yielding fewer fractions from the original sample ( 72 ). Hence, consistent with previous studies ( 53 , 73 ), we analyzed LAT1 protein through whole-muscle homogenates. In this study, LAT1 protein was reduced by 0.26 fold in the 2RDA group after the intervention, which contradicted the increased mRNA expression of LAT1/ SLC7A5 in both groups. The discrepancy may be explained through posttranslational regulation by microRNAs, which are small non-coding RNAs that can bind to mRNA to inhibit translation ( 74 ). Potentially, the discrepancy might be related to reduced necessity. By saturating the body with BCAA through the 2RDA diet, LAT1 protein may not be needed to be elevated to maintain transport capacity at fasting condition. Providing a visual image of the localization of LAT1 via immunofluorescence microscopy might provide valuable information. It has been previously shown that under basal condition, LAT1 is found in both sarcolemmal membrane and sarcoplasmic region ( 76 ), but LAT1 is only metabolically active when associated with cellular membrane ( 77 ). Unfortunately, we did not have available tissue mounted for histology in this study. Further, this study did not measure the response to a postprandial nutrient challenge, but it has been demonstrated that, postprandially, dietary protein ingestion resulted in increased arterial and intramyocellular concentrations of leucine, which corresponded with increased LAT1 expression, mTORC1 signaling and MPS ( 47 , 78 ). The lack of response to the 2RDA diet could be a result of analysis of fasting samples.

Hyperactivation of mTORC1 has been demonstrated in sarcopenic animal models ( 22 , 23 , 24 ), and in the skeletal muscle of older mice and adults when compared to young after an overnight fast ( 21 , 79 , 80 ). A downregulation of mTORC1 activity was expected due to the reduced abundance of LAT1 protein, since LAT1 influences mTORC1 signaling by regulating the uptake of leucine ( 68 ), a principle anabolic agent for the promotion of MPS ( 18 ). Analysis showed that the morning fasted mTORC1 activity was unaffected by the intervention and no change in plasma leucine concentrations was evident. However, total RPS6 increased in the 2RDA group post-intervention and when compared to the RDA group. RPS6, a component of the small (40S) ribosomal subunit ( 81 ), is the preferred substrate for p70S6K1 ( 82 ). It has been implicated in the stimulation of protein translation efficiency ( 83 ) and ribosomal synthesis ( 84 ), by interacting with transfer RNA (tRNA), initiation factors and mRNA ( 85 ). Aging has been linked to reduced translational efficiency ( 86 ), and older mice and men have less total RPS6 ( 80 ), p70S6K1 and 4E-BP1 ( 87 ) in the fasted state when compared to younger controls. The upregulation of total RPS6 in the 2RDA group could potentially be an adaptive response to increase protein translation capacity in human skeletal muscle during aging. However, there was no change in total RNA per mg of tissue, a proxy measurement of translational capacity ( 88 ). Therefore, future studies are needed to assess protein translation and ribosomal biogenesis.

The mechanistic details of the upstream events responsible for AA-dependent mTORC1 activation are complex. Several groups have proposed different mechanisms of AA sensing ( 89 , 90 ). In particular, the following targets have been proposed as AA sensors: LRS ( 35 , 36 ), Sestrin2 ( 44 , 45 ) and CASTOR1 ( 42 , 43 ). Both LRS and Sestrin2 have been proposed as leucine sensors, albeit the relationship between Sestrin2 and leucine sensing is still under debate ( 91 , 92 , 93 ). While the mRNA expression of SESN2 and its paralogs SESN1 and 3 were not affected by the dietary intervention, the mRNA expression of LRS showed a tendency to be decreased in both groups. Interestingly, acutely, EAA ingestion does not alter the postprandial expression of LRS ( 94 ) or SESN2 ( 95 , 96 ).

Sestrin2 and CASTOR1 have been proposed to regulate mTORC1 similarly ( 97 ). In the absence of leucine or arginine ( 43 , 98 ), Sestrin2 or CASTOR1 bind and inhibit GATOR2, but dissociate from it upon leucine or arginine binding. Released GATOR2 then regulates GATOR1 and Rag proteins to control the localization of mTORC1 to lysosomes ( 42 , 44 ). Although the mRNA expression of CASTOR1 showed a tendency to be greater in the 2RDA group, the expression of Rag proteins and subunits of GATOR2 ( WDR24 and MIOS ) did not change post-intervention. Instead, it has been shown that RagB protein, RRAGB , WDR24 , and MIOS increased after acute EAA supplementation ( 94 , 95 ). This suggests that the fasted expression of Rag proteins and GATOR2 may not be affected by a chronic dietary intervention. Postprandial transcriptional upregulation of AATs and mediators have repeatedly been demonstrated in human skeletal muscle to provide anabolic stimulus to mTORC1 and provide substrates for increased rates of MPS ( 30 , 99 ). Ten weeks of dietary intervention might have altered the postprandial response. To gain a better understanding of the impact of diet on anabolic signaling and AA sensing pathway, in addition to fasting condition, future studies should also examine postprandial responses.
sections.conclusion: A higher protein diet is beneficial for lean body mass maintenance ( 7 ), as increased EAA availability has been shown to activate mTORC1 signaling and MPS ( 48 , 100 ). For the first time, using muscle biopsies collected before and after a dietary protein intervention, this study demonstrated the effects of ten weeks of RDA and 2RDA protein intake on mTORC1 downstream targets, AATs, sensors and mediators proposed to be responsible for AA-dependent mTORC1 activation in older men. Following an overnight fast, LAT1 protein was reduced by a 2RDA intervention, but this did not affect the circulating concentration of leucine, mTORC1 activity or the expressions of AA sensors and mediators. However, increased total RPS6 protein could suggest improved overall translational performance to combat the loss of skeletal muscle mass commonly seen with aging.
